extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, IP professionals, policymakers and other readers seeking an overview of patent systems
extracted.subtask_description: High-level explanatory guidance on what makes an invention patentable, the applicant's disclosure obligations, how national/regional jurisdictional limits operate, the PCT international filing process, and distinctions for utility models and biotechnological deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is granted to applicants for an invention that meets the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valid for a limited period (generally 20 years). The patent system is designed to encourage innovation by providing time-limited exclusive legal rights in return for disclosure. Applicants must satisfy the substantive standards of novelty, non-obviousness (inventive step) and industrial applicability for an invention to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure obligation (sufficiency of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public, so that they may be replicated by others skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is a generally recognized requirement for receiving a patent; the application must describe the invention with sufficient detail for replication by a person skilled in the art. This disclosure is part of the exchange for time-limited exclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional scope and national/regional procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for acquiring patent rights are governed by the rules and regulations of national and regional patent offices, which issue patents and rights limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain patent rights applicants must file an application describing the invention with a national or regional office. National/regional offices apply their national law when deciding on patentability; therefore protection is jurisdiction-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT System: international filing stages and national phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can file an international application through the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) System, which facilitates acquisition of patent rights in multiple jurisdictions by delaying separate national filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT application process begins with the international phase, during which an international search and optional preliminary examination and supplementary international search are performed. It concludes with the national phase, during which national (or regional) patent offices decide on the patentability of an invention according to national law. The PCT simplifies multi-jurisdictional filing but grant decisions remain with national/regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model (UM) system differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model confers a set of rights to an invention for a limited period and differs from a traditional patent in terms and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UMs are issued for a shorter period (6–10 years) and at most offices protection is granted without substantive examination. Terms and conditions for granting a UM differ from those for granting a traditional patent; as with patents, UM procedures are governed by national IP offices and rights are limited to the issuing jurisdiction. The report treats 'utility model' to include UMs and similar short-term protections (e.g., short-term patents in Ireland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty: deposit requirement for microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention involves microorganisms, national laws in most countries require the applicant to deposit a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure plays an important role for biotechnological inventions. Depositing a microorganism sample at an IDA is commonly required to satisfy disclosure requirements in many jurisdictions.
